title: Chris Hansen Reacts to ‘Primetime’ and Robert Pattinson’s Portrayal of Him: ‘So Bizarre’ and ‘Detached From Reality’
description:
Chris Hansen finally took a seat for “Primetime,” and he was not happy about the portrayal of himself.

	The former “To Catch a Predator” host said
body:
Chris Hansen finally took a seat for “Primetime,” and he was not happy about the portrayal of himself.

	The former “To Catch a Predator” host said on Fox News’ “Jesse Watters Primetime” in August that he left the offices of distributor A24 without seeing the film due to the legal agreement they wanted him to sign. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it,” he said of the agreement. He also said he found Robert Pattinson’s impression “overly dramatic,” but that his family thought it was a “pretty good imitation.”
	

	Following a screening of Lance Oppenheim’s drama, Hansen has now shared his reactions to the full film in a 20-minute-long YouTube video posted to his channel, “Have A Seat With Chris Hansen,” on Friday.


	“It was so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” Hansen said. “Obviously, I’m not objective because the character is, you know, me, but it was so detached from reality or anything I’ve experienced then or now doing the investigations. I’m not sure what the point of it was.”

	The former host went on to criticize Pattinson’s performance, saying that “this version of Chris Hansen” was “so detached, so unhinged, so dark, so unlikeable… I mean, it’s upset my colleagues, current and former.” Hansen explained that he had about 13 members of his former crew see the film, and while some felt that the “film work was good” in terms of the story, they “got bored after the first 30 minutes.”

	Hansen also called out Oppenheim for having a “dark image of what he wanted to do,” regardless of whether it had really happened in that way, in the host’s opinion. “He wanted to create a horror-like film with interesting photography and didn’t want to hear anything else,” he said. “[He] didn’t want to have his mind polluted by anything positive that this actually achieved over the last 22 years.”
	

	He continued: “Hollywood wants to demonize the guy doing what I think is very good work that has created a dialogue that didn’t exist before and an awareness that didn’t exist before. And yet they turn him into the bad guy. And so you have to question the motives of not coming forward and talking to me or anybody who I worked closely with over the years. And they didn’t want to hear that Chris Hansen is a good guy. They didn’t want to hear that this work is important.”

	He went on to say there was not one thing he liked about the film. When asked if there were any scenes that he saw that he knew didn’t happen, he responded, “almost every one of them.” “In a way, it’s a hit piece on me and the series, which is weird,” he said.

	The film stars Pattinson as Hansen in 2006 as “To Catch a Predator” transitioned from “Dateline NBC” to its own primetime block. A24 labeled the film as “inspired by true events,” rather than a biopic.

	Pattinson himself hoped Hansen would come around on the portrayal. “I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment,” the actor said following Hansen’s comments on his imitation.

	“Primetime” opened in theaters on Friday after making its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, where it garnered buzz and a seven-minute ovation. It took second place at the box office with $8.49 million domestically.

schema.headline: Chris Hansen Reacts to ‘Primetime’ and Robert Pattinson’s Portrayal of Him: ‘So Bizarre’ and ‘Detached From Reality’

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Spoofs Oasis as Russian Hackers Who Trick Prime Minister Andy Burnham by Asking Him to Join the Band
description: Oasis and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were at the heart of a surreal cold open in the third episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2,
body:
Oasis and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were at the heart of a surreal cold open in the third episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2, where the iconic Manchester-based duo turned out to be a Russian psyop stealing Burnham’s personal details.

	The sketch started with Burnham (George Fouracres) proudly reflecting on a recent speech at the UN in New York to Secretary of State Angela Rayner (Celeste Dring).


	“It’s just like Manchester, except the trams go underground,” he said.
	

	“I tell you what, you absolutely smashed that speech to the UN,” Rayner responded. “About time someone stood up to Russia. They hate us because we have freedom and Greggs.”

	“I’m sick of Russia trying to divide us people,” Burnham said. “We can divide ourselves, thank you very much.”

	Liam (Jack Shep) and Noel Gallagher (Freddie Meredith) from Oasis then appeared and asked Burnham whether he could fill in for Liam playing the guitar at their next gig due to an injury. Burnham agreed and was asked to hand over his personal details, to which he gleefully agreed. Almost immediately, Noel and Liam Gallagher started donning Russian accents..

	“Oasis is and has always been Russian psyop,” said Noel.

	With the threat that the U.K. will now become a Russian puppet state, Burnham does not give in. “Just because you have the power to do something, doesn’t mean you should. I, for example, could hold a general election tomorrow and easily smash it,” Andy said. “But as I announced yesterday, I won’t do. And I could. Maybe I should. And I will. But I won’t. Unless I do. Which I won’t. Unless I do. And that is true leadership.”
	

	“What do you think, comrade?” asks Noel.

	“Maybe” responded Liam.

	Asked by Burnham to speak up, Noel responds to the tune of “Wonderwall”: “I said mayyyybeeee.”

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Spoofs Oasis as Russian Hackers Who Trick Prime Minister Andy Burnham by Asking Him to Join the Band

title: Chuck Varga, Founding Member of Heavy Metal Band Gwar, Dies at 68
description:
Chuck Varga, a founding member and vocalist of the heavy metal band Gwar, died on Friday following a battle with cancer. He was 68.

	Gwar bassist C
body:
Chuck Varga, a founding member and vocalist of the heavy metal band Gwar, died on Friday following a battle with cancer. He was 68.

	Gwar bassist Casey Orr announced his death in a statement shared to Facebook, writing, “Chuck Varga has left this earthly realm. He passed peacefully, his beloved wife Bambi holding his hand. He was one of a kind. As an artist, as a performer; as a scholar and gentleman. I’m better for having known him and the world is lesser for his leaving.”
	

	Orr also shared that Varga would likely be welcomed into Valhalla, a hall where soldiers go after they die in Norse mythology, by late band members Dave Brockie and Cory Smoot.


	“Raise your glass and tell his tales,” Orr concluded. “Legends never die. Hail Varga! Hail Sexicutioner!”

	While on stage, Varga would often play a character named Sexicutioner. The rock band, known for its unconventional costumes and intentionally offensive lyrics, was nominated for two Grammys, one in 1993 for Best Long Form Music Video and another in 1996 for Best Metal Performance. Gwar is currently preparing to tour this October.

	Varga’s battle with cancer became public in April, and the band organized a blood drive and fundraiser in his honor. Donors would receive a shirt designed by Varga, with Gwar’s Bob Gorman noting that Varga’s “illustrations, character designs, performances and artistic vision” continue to influence the band and his aesthetic “helped define an entire universe.”

	Varga attended Virginia Commonwealth University, where he met fellow student Hunter Jackson. The two co-founded The Slave Pit, a production space aimed toward creating student films, and its creative community ultimately led to the creation of Gwar.
	

	In 1997, Varga left the band and moved to New York City to focus his career on film, TV and Broadway. He would return to perform with Gwar intermittently until 2017, when he founded the costume and set design company Hyperreal Productions.

schema.headline: Chuck Varga, Founding Member of Heavy Metal Band Gwar, Dies at 68

title: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’
description: The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abra
body:
The Gaza documentary “NAZA” made its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival to a massive standing ovation for co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor who gave a brief Q&A with festival director Dennis Lim after the screening. Journalist and co-director Abraham told the crowd, many of whom were still drying their eyes after bearing witness in the documentary to footage of the destruction of Gaza, that it was essential to play “NAZA” at NYFF because the U.S. is responsible for funding billions to the Israeli government and supplying military aid, which is being used against the Palestinian people.
	

	“It’s important for us to see this film at this moment, as you were saying, because these older officials are talking about what is being done with taxpayer money from people sitting here,” said Abraham, who was met with cheers of approval from the audience. “This is what your country is supporting and funding… Part of the goal is to make denial of what’s going on in Gaza harder.” 


	“NAZA” first premiered at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, where it won a special jury prize and received a record-breaking 24.5-minute standing ovation. The documentary was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.” It is now set to release in more than 50 territories before becoming available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website.

	Since its premiere, the directors have come under fire from a number of Israeli officials — Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the introduction of a law that would “revoke the citizenship of anyone who slanders IDF [Israeli Defense Forces] soldiers” following the film’s debut, while Israel’s Minister of Culture threatened to revoke the filmmaker’s Israeli citizenship. 
	

	Outside the festival screening, the Israeli-American Council organized a more than 50-person protest against the film, which they described as “anti-Israel,” and said “makes serious allegations about the IDF’s conduct in the Gaza Strip while ignoring findings and information that contradict its claims.” Those in attendance gathered by LED trucks that projected footage from October 7 and portraits of those who were killed that day. 

	“It’s completely unjustified, the massacre of October 7th,” said Abraham during the Q&A. “But it also cannot justify what you’ve seen. Does it justify the slaughter of so many civilians in Gaza?”

schema.headline: ‘NAZA’ Co-Director Yuval Abraham Calls Out the U.S. Government for ‘Funding’ Israel’s Destruction of Gaza, Telling NYFF Audience: ‘This Is What Your Country Is Supporting’

title: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic
description: Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín‘s s
body:
Macabre and melancholy but suffused with a delicious absurdism that somehow doesn’t clog the arteries of its hopeful little heart, Pablo Larraín‘s sprawling, peculiar, terrific “My Sad Dead” is about 20 things at once in every moment. It’s a ghost story, obviously, on account of all the ghosts. It’s a droll tragicomedy, with eccentrically deadpan characters providing both the tragedy and the jokes. It’s a nasty body-horror and a ferocious satire — in its way as scathing a portrait of modern, urban Argentina as any of Larraín’s previous Chilean films have been about his homeland. And most surprisingly, it’s a mini-treatise on hostile urban architecture and the effect it has on the human spirit to dwell in brutal, brutalist structures that quarantine their inhabitants from society, and from each other. “Rage weighs more than concrete,” sings Shakira over the closing credits, but the Piedrabuena neighborhood of Buenos Aires is heavy with both.
	

	Ema (Mercedes Morán, in a fantastic performance of dry eyes and drier wit) is almost an emblem of Piedrabuena, though her rage has long since turned to a resilient kind of resignation, only tempered by the quick flash of amusement that often sparks up in her otherwise world-weary expression. Or should that be otherworld-weary? Ema doesn’t sleep much because of all the screaming ghosts who, for now, only she can hear. 


	A doctor who has been pushed into retirement, with dark mutterings going on about a trolley-problem decision she made regarding COVID treatments, Ema doesn’t technically live in Piedrabuena anymore — she has a spacious apartment in a nicer part of the city that she is looking to rent out. But she has recently moved back to care for her aged mother through the terminal stages of a painful illness. And that’s how we first see her, from above, as we hover like an angel or an overhead lamp, in the attic room of her mother’s house beside the Piedrabuena projects. Ema holds the bedridden woman’s frail, pale blue hand as, not particularly quietly nor entirely peacefully, she dies. Then her corpse opens its eyes.
	

	It’s not her, exactly, but a fuzzy, not-quite-opaque facsimile of her. The effect that “My Sad Dead” uses to summon the dead is the more convincing for not being particularly flashy. The unusual, low-contrast color palette that Larraín and his ace regular DP Sergio Armstrong have chosen blanches the images to a flat, pinkish gray, so that those with and without heartbeats all have the pallor of a mortuary waiting room’s magnolia walls. 

	Yet we always know who is alive and who is, well, post-alive, and not just because the dead often have a tell, like they’ll be staggering around with half their head blown off, or bleeding copiously from a ragged, ripped-open chest wound. It’s also because of their manner. Ema tends not to encounter too many quiet, dignified, expected deaths, and those who have experienced a violent end are almost childlike in their confusion and disorientation. Often they seem trapped in a cycle, doomed to re-live (and re-die) their last moments, powerless to change the outcome.

	Ema is sick of the dead and long past sick of trying to convince others that her abilities are real. So mostly she ignores the ghosts and they ignore her and that’s fine. But then her estranged sister Lidia (Alejandra Flechner) and her husband fly in for a visit from their home in Seattle, bringing with them their troubled, morbidly obese teenage daughter Julia (Carolina Álvarez), and Ema comes to realize that Julia can also commune with the dead. 

	And really commune: Julia, miserable and stigmatized and about to be committed to an institution by her hapless parents, loudly and lustily enjoys getting busy with the no-longer-with-us in a way that one supposes cannot technically be necrophilia, considering it’s sex with the spirits of the dead rather than with their bodies. Which doesn’t mean Larraín averts our gaze from these strangely moving copulations; the film is about the non-corporeal but it’s fascinated too by the flesh, by its gratification, its mortification and then, in an increasingly ethereal refrain, its slow putrefaction and decomposition.

	With its octagonal clusters of flats arranged around a central water tower that looks like a fist raised against the sky, the neighborhood doesn’t have much spirit of community. The residents occasionally gather in a disused rec center but the meetings devolve into rants about immigrants, junkies, thugs and vigilantism. One man suggests mounting the heads of thieves on spikes, a grisly image that Larraín, for once, spares us, as opposed to the bungling burglar falling from a roof and impaling himself crunchily on a railing, or the three pretty, giggling teens who get shot and shot and shot again in a gang-related hit, or the young woman who dies agonisingly of an infected dog bite she concealed because she couldn’t afford to miss work. 
	

	Ema cannot fix these restless ghosts, but sometimes she can distract them from the shock of their painful passing, a talent which puts her in demand when the water supply becomes mysteriously contaminated, and suddenly the whole of Piedrabuena can hear what she has always heard. The screams, the gunshots and the cries for help that went unanswered.

	In other hands, this would set up a supernatural TV procedural. But Ema does not solve mysteries or bring murderers to justice. “My Sad Dead” has no interest in being “Medium” and its provenance as TV — it was conceived as a Netflix miniseries but recut into this 186-minute movie for a San Sebastián competition bow — only proves that cinematic storytelling has little to do with the size of the screen on which you watch it. It is entirely cinematic, every scene loaded with texture and subtext and observational nuance. If there’s a comparison, it may be with Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog,” also nominally a television project and also one set within a single housing complex. (It feels like we’ve been talking about “Dekalog” a lot recently, given the ongoing project to remake it. Perhaps there’s something in the water.) 

	But really, the similarity is in mood and effect. Larraín, alongside Anastasia Ayazi and Guillermo Calderón, co-scripts with Mariana Enriquez, whose writings provide the foundational inspiration, and their outstanding screenplay tells a hundred little side-stories in addition to its main narrative. Almost all of them are harsh or gross or scary or sorrowful and yet the experience of “My Sad Dead” is mordantly funny and oddly uplifting. Maybe it’s the weirdness. Maybe it’s the way it makes a waterlogged ribbon of skin detaching from a shin and floating away seem deeply beautiful. Or maybe it’s just a reminder that being sad about death — your own or someone else’s — is simply an upside-down affirmation that you are happy to be alive.

schema.headline: ‘My Sad Dead’ Review: An Urban Community Gets the Haunting It Deserves in Pablo Larraín’s Superb Modern Gothic

title: Israeli Americans Protest ‘NAZA’ by Screening October 7 Footage Outside New York Premiere: ‘Compassion For Palestinian Civilians Doesn’t Require Us to Erase October 7’
description: The Israeli-American Council organized a protest Saturday afternoon outside the New York Film Festival premiere of “NAZA,” which the organization ha
body:
The Israeli-American Council organized a protest Saturday afternoon outside the New York Film Festival premiere of “NAZA,” which the organization has described as an “anti-Israel” film that “makes serious allegations about the IDF’s conduct in the Gaza Strip while ignoring findings and information that contradict its claims” and fails to present the full “context of the October 7 attack that led to the war.”

	“We mourn every innocent life lost in this war, Israeli or Palestinian. But compassion for Palestinian civilians does not require us to erase October 7, ignore Hamas or accept one narrative without questioning it,” said Noa Peri-Jensch, chief communities officer of the Israeli-American Council (IAC). “This is why we are here today: not to prevent anyone from speaking, but to make sure that our voices, our experiences and the truth are being heard as well.”
	

	“NAZA,” which was shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” recently won a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival. The documentary is now set to release in more than 50 territories before becoming available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website.


	As “NAZA” screened inside Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall, more than 50 protesters gathered outside the venue, where mobile LED trucks projected graphic footage from October 7 and portraits of those who were killed that day. Demonstrators carried various versions of signs that read, “LEARN THE FACTS. KNOW THE TRUTH.” There was also an additional security presence outside the venue, with over a dozen police officers on watch. 
	



	

	



	Peri-Jensch introduced Rom El-Hai, a survivor of the Oct. 7 attack on the Nova music festival. He said “it doesn’t surprise [him]” that the New York Film Festival would screen a film made by “traitors” to the Israeli cause.“If there is someone here who wants to make a film about genocide, about hatred, brutality and killing innocent people, all the material is here,” El-Hai said, flashing his phone to the crowd. “I took pictures of everything. I saw the hatred with my own eyes.”

	Karen Toledano, a protestor who stood in solidarity with the IAC, expressed that she feels like Israeli voices “have been stifled” within the creative community“I feel like our voices have been stifled in spaces that have called themselves inclusive for many years,” Toledano said. “Sometimes when I do try to have a calm conversation and I’m encountered with anger, I know in my head that there just isn’t an argument on the other side. But it doesn’t make it any easier to swallow when really all you want to do is talk about the facts and set the record straight.”



	

	



	On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a defiant address to the U.N. General Assembly, which prompted a mass walkout of delegates who left the room when his speech began, “Where were you when the Iranian tyrants butchered and maimed tens of thousands of unarmed Iranian civilians?”

	Hundreds of pro-Palestine protestors gathered outside the United Nations building, resulting in roughly 100 arrests, including Hannah Einbinder and Susan Sarandon.

	“The U.S. government has the power to bring an end to all of this killing, pillaging, and land theft, yet instead it chooses to welcome the butcher of Gaza with open arms,” Einbinder wrote online after being released from detention. “The fact that the orchestrator of all this bloodshed is roaming freely in our cities is an indictment of BOTH REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS who enable and protect architects of genocide like Netanyahu. Let us not mistake the spectacle for the story: genocide is the headline, and it is time for it to end.”

schema.headline: Israeli Americans Protest ‘NAZA’ by Screening October 7 Footage Outside New York Premiere: ‘Compassion For Palestinian Civilians Doesn’t Require Us to Erase October 7’

title: Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Wins Big at San Sebastián, as ‘La Bola Negra’ and ‘NAZA’ Take Audience Awards
description: “Tender Loving Care,” the latest and purportedly last film by veteran British writer-director Mike Leigh, was allegedly turned down for a Competitio
body:
“Tender Loving Care,” the latest and purportedly last film by veteran British writer-director Mike Leigh, was allegedly turned down for a Competition slot at the Venice Film Festival — but it had the last laugh at San Sebastián, ruling the Spanish festival’s awards ceremony with three prizes in the main competition, including the Golden Shell for Best Film.

	The jury, headed by U.S. filmmaker Ira Sachs, was so enamored of the intimate character drama about social and familial care that they handed Leigh a second win for Best Screenplay, while ensemble standout Kate O’Flynn — fresh from her Emmy victory for “Widow’s Bay” — was one of two women awarded the non-gendered Best Lead Performance prize, for her funny, gradually heartbreaking performance as a put-upon London social worker facing up to the ailing health of her own parents. 
	

	Neither Leigh nor O’Flynn was present at the ceremony, though both sent video acceptance speeches: Leigh, keeping it brief, concluded his acceptance with a simple “thank you, thank you and love to everybody,” while O’Flynn celebrated “Tender Loving Care” as “[a] film that sees empathy as a strength and the attempt to care important.” She further dedicated her award to Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson and Alice Bailey Johnson, her three co-stars in an equally weighted quartet. Jesson and Bailey Johnson, meanwhile, were on hand to accept Leigh’s screenplay award on his behalf, with Jesson addressing the “misunderstanding” that the director’s films are improvised, praising the “precision, rigor and purpose” of Leigh’s shooting process.
	

	Another multiple prizewinner was Norwegian director Hans Petter Moland’s handsome rural epic “Growth of the Soil,” which was recently selected as Norway’s submission for the Best International Feature Oscar. Its star Asta Kamma August, daughter of the filmmaker Bille August, shared the Best Lead Performance  award with O’Flynn for her affecting turn as one half of a young couple building a farmstead from scratch in the early 20th century. Oskar Dahlsbakken won Best Cinematography for his sturdy lensing of the film’s craggily spectacular Nordic mountainscapes.

	Also awarded by the jury — which in addition to Sachs, included actors Bill Skarsgård, Alice Braga and Patricia López Arnaiz, producer Mike Goodridge, filmmaker Genki Kawamura and screenwriter Catherine Paillé — was “Border,” a short, striking and sexually explicit debut feature by Hong Kong filmmaker Ah Biao, which won the Special Jury Prize for its originality and daring. Swedish Sámi filmmaker Amanda Kernell won Best Director for “Brace Your Heart,” a portrait of a young female reindeer herder in the indigenous Sámi community, which also picked up a special mention in Toronto’s Platform competition last week. In an impassioned speech, Kernell explained her deeply personal motivation for making the film, which she said she hoped would “heal old wounds, especially in my family.”

	With only five of the 17 films in competition taking prizes, high-profile titles going home empty-handed included Fatih Akin’s festival opener “Ghost Song,” Pablo Larraín’s “My Sad Dead,” Fred Cavayé’s all-star “Les Miserables” adaptation and Jesse Eisenberg’s fall festival favorite “The Debut.” The only Spanish winner in competition, meanwhile, was veteran character actor Javier Cámara, a popular Best Supporting Performance pick for his turn in the comic fantasy “5 More Minutes.” After three consecutive years of Spanish films taking the Golden Shell, this year marks a slightly disappointing turnout for the home team.

	But national pride was bolstered by the Audience Award for Best Film — which went, to absolutely no one’s surprise, to local favorites Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi for their queer epic “La Bola Negra,” one week after the international festival sensation took the People’s Choice Award at Toronto. A second Audience Award for Best European Film — which presumably discounts the main award winner — went to docmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor for “NAZA,” their searing exposé of Israeli war crimes in Gaza, which won the Jury Prize at Venice earlier this month. It’s the second year in a row that San Sebastián audiences have shown their solidarity with the pro-Palestinian movement: Last year’s Audience Award went to Kaouther Ben Hania’s eventually Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”
	

	Several of the night’s winners, moreover, expressed their support for the people of Palestine on stage. August, pointing to the pro-Palestine pin on her dress, concluded her speech by saying, “No one is free until everyone is free — free Palestine.” Meanwhile, German filmmaker Naëmi Ada offered a similarly worded sentiment with a more pointed kicker in her acceptance of the New Directors award: “There is no individual liberation without collective liberation,” she said, adding, “I condemn the complicity of the German state in the genocide.”

	Ada’s debut feature “Body of Glass” — a dark psychological drama about a young dancer who immerses herself in a stranger’s grieving circle — was the top prizewinner in New Directors, the festival’s separate competition for first-time filmmakers; a special mention went to “The World Before,” a coming-of-age romance by South Korean director Yoon Dan-bi.

	Top prizes in the festival’s two other competitive sections went to titles that have already gathered significant acclaim on the festival circuit. Argentine-American photographer-turned-filmmaker Alessandra Sanguinetti won the top prize in the Latin Horizons strand for her feature documentary “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer,” shot over the course of more than 20 years in rural Argentina, which won multiple awards, including Best First Film, at Locarno in August. 

	In the more experimentally-oriented Zabaltegi-Tabakalera competition, Jane Schoenbrun emerged victorious for her delicious summer cult item “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” — a film she described, in her video acceptance speech, as “a celebration of being a little freak, and also a celebration of cinema.” The first statement is a far cry from anything one can imagine Mike Leigh saying; the second, at San Sebastián, felt a more universal ideal.

	Full list of award winners:OFFICIAL SELECTION AWARDSGolden Shell for Best Film: “Tender Loving Care,” Mike LeighSpecial Jury Prize: “Border,” Ah Biao 

	Silver Shell for Best Director: “Brace Your Heart,” Amanda KernellSilver Shell for Best Leading Performance: “Tender Loving Care,” Kate O’Flynn; “Growth of the Soil,” Asta Kamma AugustSilver Shell for Best Supporting Performance: “5 More Minutes,” Javier CámaraJury Prize for Best Cinematography: “Growth of the Soil,” Oskar Dahlsbakken

title: Marine Atlan’s French Oscar Hopeful ‘La Gradiva’ Takes Top Prizes at 30th Queer Lisboa – the Biggest Edition to Date
description: French filmmaker Marine Atlan’s lauded debut film “La Gradiva” proved the big winner at the 30th Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival, t
body:
French filmmaker Marine Atlan’s lauded debut film “La Gradiva” proved the big winner at the 30th Queer Lisboa – International Queer Film Festival, taking the best feature film and Audience Awards.

	A sweeping portrait of the vicissitudes of youth, the film, which also won the top prize at the Cannes Critics’ Week, follows a group of French students on a final-year school trip to Pompeii, led by a passionate teacher eager to instill in them cultural and historical appreciation.
	

	Lorena Ros’ Spanish documentary “Up and Running” (“Corren las Liebres”) likewise scored best documentary and Audience Awards. The film offers a candid look at the growing marginalization and homelessness amongst the trans ex-prisoner population in Barcelona.


	This year’s festival, which closed Saturday with a screening of Leah Nelson’s animated feature film “Tangles,” was the most popular ever, attracting the highest number of attendees in its history, with more than 11,500 admissions at the festival’s 67 screenings over nine days — a 53% increase over 2025.

	“This edition of the festival was particularly rewarding for us,” Queer Lisboa artistic director João Ferreira told Variety. “We surpassed the historic milestone of 11,500 spectators, the highest attendance ever recorded in our festival. And it was equally rewarding because we saw the audience respond to a particularly ambitious film program, which we put together to mark our 30th anniversary, from the retrospective — which was also one of the most extensive in our history in terms of number of screenings — to the many films from the major European festivals that we managed to premiere in Portugal.
	

	“Having started the festival in 1997 as the first film festival in Lisbon, and still going strong, despite the many adversities we faced in these three decades, this really shows the artistic and political pertinence of queer cinema,” Ferreira added.

	Indeed, with a program strongly characterized by themes of family, romantic and sexual relationships and a hopeful future, the festival team highlighted throughout the event the excellent shape of contemporary queer cinema and  in particular the impressive range of the 2026 harvest of new films, which led to nine sold-out screenings, notably of “The Man I Love,” “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” “Bitter Christmas,” “The Faggots & Their Friends Between Revolutions,” “Orlando,” “La conscience politique,” “The Passion According to GHB” and “Jim Queen.”

	In awarding “La Gradiva” the festival’s top prize, the jury, comprised of cultural manager Kathleen Gomes, film programmer Maria João Madeira and actor Miguel Nunes, said the film was “a journey to a contemporary Italy that follows a group of teenagers at a decisive moment in their transition to adulthood. Amidst ruins, tectonic shifts and the vibrancy of nature, the characters question themselves, fall in love and hurt one another, navigating a landscape as ancient as it is unstable. The archaeology of history, the formation of identities and the search for a sense of belonging converge as the vital force behind this dazzling debut work, which touches on the fragility of human nature.”

	Variety’s Jessica Kiang wrote in her review: “Seismically sensitive and deeply moving, Atlan’s film is simply one of the most piercingly accurate and immersive portrayals ever, of that fleeting moment when — not really a kid but still, really, a kid — you are simultaneously the most forcibly socialized and possibly the loneliest you will ever be.”

	“La Gradiva” is one the five finalists in the race to be France’s entry for this best international feature Oscar. The film will be released Stateside via 1-2 Special and is being handled in Portugal by NOS Audiovisuais.



	

					Up and Running (Corren las Liebres)
									Courtesy of Queer Lisboa
	



	Commenting on its selection of “Up and Running” as best doc, the jury — comprising film programmer Diana Cipriano, journalist Filipe Santa-Bárbara and Luis Rosado from the RTP2 editorial team — said the film won “for the generosity and respect shown through the camera’s lens, for the magnetism of the women it portrays, particularly Noa, and the way it allows their character to rise above all their vulnerabilities.”
	

	In the same section, the jury also awarded a special mention to Nông Nhật Quang’s Vietnamese doc “Baby Jackfruit Baby Guava.” The film, which premiered at Visions du Réel, journeys into the past through the director’s diaries and family photographs.



	

					Nuestro Cuerpo Es una Estrella que Se Expande
									Courtesy of Queer Lisboa
	



	Mexican documentary “Nuestro Cuerpo Es una Estrella que Se Expande,” by siblings Semillites Hernández Velasco and Tania Hernández Velasco, a reflection on trans sensibilities intertwined with the landscape and family ties, won the top prize in the Queer Art Competition, a section dedicated to works that explore the boundaries of cinematic languages and genres.

	The jury, comprising Brazilian director Leonardo Mouramateus, curator Marta Mestre and German filmmaker Matthias Müller, also awarded a special mention to “Life Is About Losing Everything,” by brothers Benjamin Ramírez Pérez and Stefan Ramírez Pérez, “a fascinating and colorful hybrid that serves as an adaptation of the highly distinctive universe of Canadian poet and feminist writer Lynn Crosbie,” presented as a world premiere at the festival.



	

					Je veux qu’on se souvienne de nous
									Courtesy of Hutong Productions, Le Bal
	



	In the Short Film Competition, “Je veux qu’on se souvienne de nous,” by French writer Hélène Giannecchini, won the best short award, while “Fronteriza,” a Brazilian-Paraguayan production by Nay Mendl and Rosa Caldeira, won the AltContent Award.

	Taking the top prize in the In My Shorts Competition, dedicated to short films from European film schools, was “Ãsheghetam,” a French-Swiss-Iranian production by Iranian filmmaker Filmsaaz.

	Across both sections, the festival screened 32 short films, judged by Brazilian cinematographer Aline Belfort, filmmaker Caio Amado Soares and programmer Lou Loução.

title: Amelia Dimoldenberg Jokes About Why ‘Chicken Shop Date’ Is Ending in ‘SNL U.K.’ Monologue: ‘Celebrities Weren’t Coming on to Date Me. They Were Coming on to Promote Their Work!’
description: Earlier this month, Amelia Dimoldenberg revealed that her popular celebrity interview series, “Chicken Shop Date,” would be coming to an end. And in
body:
Earlier this month, Amelia Dimoldenberg revealed that her popular celebrity interview series, “Chicken Shop Date,” would be coming to an end. And in her monologue as the host of “SNL U.K.” on Saturday night, she playfully gave some insight as to why.

	“I found out something devastating. Apparently, these celebrities weren’t coming on to date me,” Dimoldenberg joked. “They were coming on to promote their work!”


	She added, “It makes so much more sense now. Andrew Garfield had a film out! When he kept saying, ‘I’m looking forward to the big release,’ I thought that was a sex thing.” 
	

	She then took aim at Ed Sheeran, who has drawn controversy over the last couple of weeks for dropping Macklemore from his tour after a political speech in which he said “free Palestine.” 

	“I’m incredibly privileged to have done so many interviews with people like Idris Elba, Cher, and even a world famous red-headed puppet with a hand up his arse telling him what to say,” she said as an image of Elmo appeared. 

	“No, the other one!” she quipped as Sheeran’s face flashed on screen. 

	Dimoldenberg ended her monologue by reminiscing about her early days at a youth center in London, which taught her that “I am an awkward girl, and there’s no shame in that. Just huge profit.” 

	She continued: “I am proof that you don’t have to stop being awkward to be successful … I am proof that you should always be yourself. Be yourself on ‘Chicken Shop Date.’ Be yourself on the Oscars red carpet. Be yourself in ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2.’ Be yourself in your upcoming rom-com. Be yourself in all of the sketches during ‘Saturday Night Live U.K.'”
	

	Just like the chickens I love to eat,” Dimoldenberg concluded, “you don’t have to have range.” 

	Watch her full monologue below.

title: Sylvester Stallone Opens Up About Severe Anxiety & Recurring Attacks
description:
Sylvester Stallone
                          My First Anxiety-Induced Attack Nearly KO'd Me!
body:
Sylvester Stallone
                          My First Anxiety-Induced Attack Nearly KO'd Me!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 26, 2026
                            12:44 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 26, 2026
                                3:07 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how he's quietly suffered anxiety-induced attacks for decades ... and how his diagnosis still plays a part in his life.
      
    
            In a wide-ranging, candid interview with The New York Times, Sylvester said the first time he suffered from an anxiety-induced attack was when he was watching daily footage from a film project in his mid-30s.
      
    
            He said ... "The first time was when I was 36 and I was watching dailies, and then all of a sudden I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out. And bang, down I went. Took a knee, crawled, rolled over, and now I’m in this dark movie theater."
      
    
            While Sylvester didn't label the episodes as panic attacks ... he did say he suffered similar moments of crippling anxiety "again and again and again."
      
    
            The "Rocky" star said that the attacks come out of nowhere ... and are something he still deals with as he gets older.
      
    
            He said ... "When I’m in a crowd, I’d be with my wife at an art exhibition and the room is filling up. It’s getting more and more, and then I’d go, 'I'm going down,' and she’d be like, 'Let’s get out of here.' And literally I just make it to the alley, boom, get down on one knee."

            Kaia Gerber is leaning on her friends for support after her late brother Presley Gerber's death certificate was released ... as a new pic shows her hanging out with a pal.
      
    
            In the photo ... Kaia and a friend -- who were both wearing sunglasses -- can be seen arriving together at her Hollywood Hills home Friday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We reported earlier ... Kaia's dad Rande Gerber was seen showing up to Presley's Los Angeles home after news broke that Presley had been cremated.
      

            Kaia's pals have been continuously showing up for the actress.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After the model's cat Tony went missing earlier this week, her friends Jake Shane, Lewis Pullman and Carissa Gallo canvassed the area of the lost pet.
      
    
            And it seems their efforts paid off ... as we reported that her cat was delivered to Kaia safe and sound thanks to the missing cat flyers.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Presley -- who was discovered dead inside his room after a suspected overdose at a sober living facility in Santa Monica -- was only 27.
      
    
            TMZ learned police are investigating his death as an overdose ... and a preliminary investigation is ongoing before an official cause of death is released.
